Tools for this journey emergency fund calculator → How to Ask Chase to Reverse Outage Fees Asking Chase directly to review and refund charges tied to downtime requires clear documentation and prompt communication. Follow these five steps to submit your request: Identify and list every fee that posted around the November 16 window, noting the exact date, transaction description, and dollar figure. Gather supporting proof, including screenshots of app error messages, connection failure notices from linked tools, and account statements showing attempted payment dates. Contact Chase by phone or in writing through your Chase account. Record the date and time of every conversation, the name or identification number of each representative you speak with, and any reference number assigned to your case. Follow up in writing through your Chase account if you spoke by phone, confirming the details discussed and providing attached copies of your documentation. Submitting this request does not guarantee that Chase will reverse the charge. Each fee reversal remains subject to individual review by Chase. What Chase Said Happened on November 16 According to reporting by NBC News , Chase customers reported trouble logging into accounts and withdrawing funds on Monday, November 16, 2026. Around 4:00 p.m. on X, JPMorganChase said it experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system. Chase confirmed that the problem was not cyber-related. Chase stated that customers still had access to accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal. The disruption affected online services as well as in-person branch transactions across an institution serving approximately 94 million customer relationships, 5,000 branches, and 15,000 automated teller machines (ATMs). A Chase spokesperson told NBC News around 6:30 p.m. that transactions were posting normally. The report did not state that service was fully restored. Fortune reported that the system problem spread across the Chase website and mobile application to certain branches and third-party financial applications. Plaid noted that its own network operated normally but observed connection problems communicating with Chase accounts, which caused errors when users attempted to link or refresh accounts. A Chase spokesperson told Fortune that technical problems slowed completion times for transactions. In 2010, Chase online banking was down for more than a day. Fortune reports that Chase then agreed to refund late fees to customers who missed payments, if they called to ask. That past decision serves as historical precedent rather than a binding commitment for 2026. Which Fees to Look For Review your account statements carefully to identify any charges assessed while systems were delayed. The table below details the published terms under the Chase Overdraft Services terms: Fee Type Amount Rule and Conditions Standard overdraft fee $34 Charged per item covered at Chase discretion; maximum 3 fees per business day ($102 daily cap) Transactions of $5 or less $0 No fee charged if the transaction amount is $5 or less Overdrawn by $50 or less at day's end $0 No fee charged if the account is overdrawn by $50 or less at the end of the business day Chase Overdraft Assist $0 If overdrawn by more than $50, no fee applies if you deposit enough funds to bring the balance to $50 or less overdrawn by 11:00 p.m. ET (8:00 p.m. PT) the next business day Debit Card Coverage OFF $0 Everyday debit card transactions are declined when funds are insufficient, preventing overdraft fees Debit Card Coverage ON $34 Everyday debit card transactions may be approved at Chase discretion, incurring the standard fee Chase Secure Banking $0 Checking account that Chase describes as having no overdraft fees The checked sources do not publish specific dollar amounts for late fees or non-sufficient funds (NSF) charges. Do not assume a fixed dollar rate for those items. If delayed transaction posting caused a late fee, add that specific line item to your itemized review list. What to Document and a Request Script Before speaking to a representative, organize your evidence so you can state the facts clearly. Keep copies of the following items: The dates and exact times you attempted to access your account, transfer funds, or make payments. Account statement lines displaying the posted fees alongside the underlying transactions. Screenshots of mobile application errors, website timeout pages, or third-party transfer alerts. Records showing sufficient funds were present or intended for deposit before the disruption began. A contact log listing the date, time, representative name or ID, and ticket reference number for every interaction. Use this request script as a guide when calling customer service or writing a message through your Chase account: "I am contacting you to request a fee reversal for charges caused by the technical outage on November 16, 2026. As a direct result, my account was assessed a fee on [Date] in the amount of [Dollar Amount]. I attempted to complete this transaction during the downtime, and the delay was outside my control. Please review my account history, waive this charge, and confirm the adjustment in writing." State the facts without asserting that Chase is legally mandated to grant the waiver. Focus on showing that your account remained in good standing prior to the system failure. Delayed Zelle Payments and Electronic Transfer Errors Account holders who attempted person-to-person transfers during the disruption faced delays. In a statement reported by NBC News, Zelle stated: "Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should. An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly." Because the transfer delays stemmed from processing at the financial institution rather than the central payment network, resolution requires working directly through Chase. If you believe an electronic fund transfer was handled incorrectly, federal rules provide a formal procedure. Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005.11 ) lists the errors it covers. Three are an unauthorized electronic fund transfer, an incorrect transfer to or from your account, and a transfer missing from your periodic statement. The financial institution must investigate if you submit an oral or written notice of error no later than 60 days after the institution sends the periodic statement displaying the disputed item. Your error notice must provide your name and account number, along with the type, date, and dollar amount of the suspected error. Chase may require written confirmation within 10 business days of receiving an oral notice. Chase must decide within 10 business days whether an error occurred, or take up to 45 days if it grants a provisional credit for the disputed amount within the initial 10 business days. Longer periods of 20 business days and 90 days apply to some new accounts and to certain point-of-sale and foreign transfers (12 CFR 1005.11(c)(3)). The sources checked do not state whether outage-related processing delays or incidental bank fees qualify as errors under Regulation E. Treat your request for a fee refund as a direct appeal to Chase rather than a statutory error claim unless a specific transfer posted for the wrong amount. When to Escalate to the CFPB If Chase refuses to refund fees resulting from the system downtime or fails to provide an answer, you can submit a formal complaint to the CFPB. The CFPB routes submitted consumer complaints directly to financial companies for a response. According to published CFPB complaint procedures, most companies provide an initial response within 15 days, and in some cases give a final response within 60 days. Before submitting a complaint, contact Chase first, as the CFPB complaint guide suggests. When compiling your complaint, include only the most important dates, fee figures, and communication logs. You may upload supporting attachments such as monthly statements, transaction receipts, and customer service correspondence, up to a maximum file limit of 50 pages. You generally cannot file a second CFPB complaint about the same problem. Put every date, fee and document in the first one. The CFPB enters complaint details, excluding direct personal identifiers, into its public Consumer Complaint Database. Once Chase submits its official response through the system, you have 60 days to provide consumer feedback on the outcome. You can file online through the complaint portal or call the agency directly at (855) 411-2372. Our Takeaway Ask Chase to reverse each fee tied to the November 16 outage. Document transaction times and reference numbers, and submit a CFPB complaint if Chase leaves the charges in place. The checked sources do not show that Chase must reverse a fee. A Regulation E error notice is a separate route that applies only if an electronic fund transfer was unauthorized, incorrect, or omitted. These steps apply directly to charges triggered by system downtime, though any future announcement from Chase regarding automatic refunds or blanket waivers would supersede individual requests. The Minnesota Department of Revenue (DOR) announced that preliminary property tax levies statewide could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, which is a 6.5% increase. Each local authority's final levy is generally capped at its preliminary levy, but your final tax bill can still be higher or lower than the notice shows because of items excluded by law and changes to your property's valuation or classification. County treasurers mail these notices every November. They give owners time to review proposed spending before city councils, county boards and school boards vote on final levies. Under Minnesota Statutes 275.065 , the notice breaks down what each local taxing authority proposes to collect, lists public meeting dates and provides contact details for public comment. Reviewing the notice line by line shows which local government is driving any tax increase and tells you where to direct your feedback before final levies are certified by December 28, 2026. Tools for this journey home affordability calculator → What a Truth-in-Taxation Notice Means for Your Tax Bill A Truth-in-Taxation notice is a parcel-specific estimate of your property taxes for the coming year based on preliminary levies adopted by your local taxing authorities. It is not a bill, and you do not make a payment from it. The county treasurer mails the notice by first class mail after November 10 and on or before November 24. It goes to each taxpayer at the address on the county assessment roll. You can ask in writing for electronic delivery. In its press release , the Minnesota Department of Revenue says preliminary levies statewide show property taxes could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, representing a 6.5% overall increase. The Department of Revenue says final levies can be set lower, but not higher, than preliminary levies. Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 6(a) lists limited exceptions. However, your individual parcel's bill could be more or less than the figure shown on the notice. The estimate does not account for certain items excluded by statute, such as special assessments or voter-approved referenda passed after the proposed levies were certified. You can take concrete steps right now: Compare the current-year tax column against the proposed tax column for each local taxing authority. Identify which specific entity, such as your county, city or school district, is proposing the largest dollar or percentage change. Note the meeting dates, times and locations listed on the notice for the authorities responsible for the increase. Attend the public budget meetings between late November and late December to ask questions and comment on proposed spending. Submit written comments directly to the taxing authority using the mailing address, phone number or official website printed on your notice if you cannot attend in person. Final levies must be set by local governments by December 28, 2026. The Department of Revenue then compiles the adopted levies and releases final property tax levy information in February. Why Proposed Taxes Are Rising in 2027 According to the Minnesota Department of Revenue , preliminary figures show property taxes statewide could increase by a maximum of $949 million over 2026, a 6.5% increase. Last year, the final statewide levy increase was $74 million lower than preliminary levies, resulting in a final annual increase of 6.4%. Preliminary levy changes vary significantly depending on the category of taxing authority: Taxing authority type 2026 final levy 2027 preliminary levy Proposed percent change Cities $3.985 billion $4.309 billion 8.1% Counties $4.520 billion $4.887 billion 8.1% Townships $350 million $367 million 4.9% Schools $4.378 billion $4.599 billion 5.0% Special taxing districts $544 million $564 million 3.7% Local-government groups point to budget pressure. As reported by CBS Minnesota , property taxes could rise by nearly $1 billion statewide, though how much an individual homeowner pays depends on local tax rates and property value. In county-level proposals, Hennepin County pitched an 8.1% levy increase, while Dakota County proposed an 18.5% increase. John McCarthy, chief financial officer of the League of Minnesota Cities, stated that cities are down to "bread-and-butter basic services". He said property taxes are "really the only tool that cities have left." Matt Hilgart of the Minnesota Association of Counties cited changes to Medicaid and food assistance under federal law taking effect, which shift costs to counties. The Minnesota Legislature provided one-time property tax relief of $125 million earlier this year. The Department of Revenue also notes that individual Truth-in-Taxation notices do not include the results of November 3, 2026, ballot referenda for operations or capital projects held across 63 school districts. Statewide, 26 of those 63 school referenda passed at least partially. The summarized preliminary data includes these referendum results, but Truth-in-Taxation notices do not include them. How to Read the Notice, Column by Column The layout of your Truth-in-Taxation notice is governed by Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3 . The document displays parcel data alongside an itemized comparison between current-year property taxes and proposed property taxes for each taxing jurisdiction serving your home. Notice element Statutory reference What is displayed on your notice Market value Subd. 3(d) County assessor market value on November 1 for the current tax year and next year; stated as final values. Property classification Subd. 3(d) Classifies the parcel as homestead or nonhomestead residential property. County tax Subd. 3(d) Actual current-year tax paid to the county alongside the proposed county tax amount. City or town tax Subd. 3(d) Actual current-year tax paid to the municipality alongside the proposed municipal tax. State general tax Subd. 3(d) Displays the state general tax; proposed equals final. School district levies Subd. 3(d) Separates voter-approved school operating levies from other local school board levies. Tax credits Subd. 3(d) Displays the agricultural homestead credit or school building bond credit where applicable. Special taxing districts Subd. 3(d) Shows the sum of special taxing districts. Total proposed tax Subd. 3(d) Sum of all taxing authorities showing dollar difference and overall percentage change. Hearing information Subd. 3(c) Meeting dates, times and physical addresses where budgets and levies will be discussed. Authority contact details Subd. 3(c) Official website URLs, telephone contact numbers and mailing addresses for comments. Where tax increment financing or the metropolitan fiscal disparities areawide tax applies to a property, those items are stated separately on the form. If a school referendum was pending at the time the notice was drafted, the notice includes a specific note warning that the final school tax amount may be higher than shown if voters approved the measure. Keep the statutory calendar in mind as you review the notice: November 10 to November 24: County treasurers print and deliver notices by first class mail. November 25 to December 28: Required public budget meetings take place across qualifying local jurisdictions. December 28, 2026: Deadline for local governments to set final 2027 property tax levies. February 2027: The Department of Revenue compiles local certifications and releases final statewide levy data. How to Use the Hearing Public budget meetings give taxpayers a direct forum to review spending decisions before local elected officials take a final binding vote. Under Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(c) , mandatory public hearings must be held by counties, cities with a population over 500, school districts, regional library authorities, metropolitan taxing districts and certain fire protection and emergency medical services special taxing districts. According to the Department of Revenue Truth-in-Taxation guidelines , these public meetings must take place between November 25 and December 28, 2026. The statute specifies that meetings must be scheduled after November 24 and must not begin before 6:00 p.m. To find the exact date, time and room location for your city council, county board or school district, check the meeting details printed directly on your parcel notice. At these meetings, the taxing authority discusses its budget and levy, and members of the public must be allowed to speak. If you plan to attend, prepare concise remarks focused on specific budget line items or tax percentage changes shown on your notice. Bring your mailed document to verify the proposed dollar increase for that jurisdiction. If you are unable to attend the scheduled public hearing, use the website, phone number or mailing address printed on the form to submit written comments to elected board members before the final levy certification on December 28. What the Hearing Can and Cannot Change Attending a Truth-in-Taxation meeting allows you to advocate for lower spending before final budgets are locked in, but the meeting has distinct legal limits. Local elected officials can choose to adopt a final levy that is lower than the preliminary levy based on public input. Under Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 6(a) , the final levy certified by a city, county, school district, regional library district or metropolitan special taxing district cannot exceed its proposed levy, with limited statutory exceptions: A school district levy where voters approved an operating or capital referendum after the preliminary levy was certified. A city or county levy approved by voters in a referendum after preliminary certification. A levy for principal and interest on voter-approved bonds. State-approved funding needs for natural disaster repairs, if the commissioner of revenue approves. Final tort judgments rendered against the municipality that became final after preliminary levies were set, if the commissioner of revenue approves. Changes to statutory levy limits certified after the initial proposed levy deadline. Subdivision 6(a) also allows amounts for emergency debt certificates and state unallotment. Subdivision 6(b) says the cap does not apply to towns or to special taxing districts other than regional library and metropolitan districts. Under subdivisions 3(c) and 3(d), a town or the state general tax is final at its proposed amount, and a town can change its levy at a special town meeting under section 365.52. The public hearing cannot change your property's assessed value or tax classification. Assessor records as of November 1 establish the market value listed on your notice. If you believe your property is incorrectly classified as nonhomestead when it is your primary residence, Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(g) provides relief. If you give the county assessor satisfactory documentation by the applicable deadline, and the home qualified for homestead status in that assessment year, the assessor must reclassify the property as homestead for taxes payable in 2027. The statute does not give the deadline date, so ask your county assessor for it. Additionally, under subdivision 3(e), the law mandates that your notice explicitly state that proposed and final taxes do not include special assessments, natural disaster cleanup costs, final tort judgments, contamination taxes or voter-approved referenda passed after certified proposals. Because these exclusions exist, never treat the total proposed figure as a ceiling on your final tax bill. Your ultimate property tax bill could be more or less than the notice indicates. Our Takeaway For Minnesota homeowners with a proposed-tax notice, remember that this document is a preliminary estimate rather than a bill. Each taxing authority's final levy is generally capped at its proposed levy. The Department of Revenue says final levies can be lower but not higher than preliminary levies. Your final bill can still differ. Subdivision 3(e) exclusions such as special assessments and post-certification referenda move it, and so do separate valuation and classification decisions. Compare the current and proposed numbers for each taxing district, identify which entity is driving the change and attend that authority's public hearing before final votes are cast. Then attend your local budget hearing before December 28 to give your input on spending. Frequently asked questions Is a Truth-in-Taxation notice a bill? No, a Truth-in-Taxation notice is not a bill, and you do not pay the amount listed. It is a parcel-specific proposal showing what your property taxes would be if local taxing authorities adopt their preliminary budgets. Can my property tax go up after the notice? Yes, your final tax bill could be more or less than the proposed amount. While local authorities generally cannot raise their final levies above preliminary numbers, final tax bills can rise due to items excluded from the notice, including special assessments, later voter-approved referenda, disaster cleanup levies and final tort judgments. When are final levies set? According to the Minnesota Department of Revenue, local governments must set final 2027 property tax levies by December 28, 2026. The Minnesota Department of Revenue compiles those local certifications and publishes final property tax levy information in February 2027. Which governments must hold a hearing? Counties, school districts, regional library authorities, metropolitan taxing districts, certain fire protection and emergency medical services special taxing districts and cities with populations over 500 must hold a public hearing between November 25 and December 28, 2026. What does the notice leave out? Under Minnesota law, the notice excludes special assessments, voter-approved referenda passed after proposed taxes are certified, post-certification disaster cleanup costs, post-certification tort judgments and contamination taxes on remediated property. What if my notice lists my home as nonhomestead? If your primary residence is listed as nonhomestead, contact your county assessor immediately. Under Minnesota Statutes 275.065 subdivision 3(g), providing satisfactory documentation to the county assessor by the applicable deadline requires the assessor to reclassify qualifying property as homestead for the upcoming tax year. mainEntity.name: Is a Truth-in-Taxation notice a bill?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, a Truth-in-Taxation notice is not a bill, and you do not pay the amount listed. It is a parcel-specific proposal showing what your property taxes would be if local taxing authorities adopt their preliminary budgets.

mainEntity.name: Can my property tax go up after the notice?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, your final tax bill could be more or less than the proposed amount. While local authorities generally cannot raise their final levies above preliminary numbers, final tax bills can rise due to items excluded from the notice, including special assessments, later voter-approved referenda, disaster cleanup levies and final tort judgments.

mainEntity.name: When are final levies set?

acceptedAnswer.text: According to the Minnesota Department of Revenue, local governments must set final 2027 property tax levies by December 28, 2026. The Minnesota Department of Revenue compiles those local certifications and publishes final property tax levy information in February 2027.

mainEntity.name: Which governments must hold a hearing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Counties, school districts, regional library authorities, metropolitan taxing districts, certain fire protection and emergency medical services special taxing districts and cities with populations over 500 must hold a public hearing between November 25 and December 28, 2026.

mainEntity.name: What does the notice leave out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under Minnesota law, the notice excludes special assessments, voter-approved referenda passed after proposed taxes are certified, post-certification disaster cleanup costs, post-certification tort judgments and contamination taxes on remediated property.

mainEntity.name: What if my notice lists my home as nonhomestead?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your primary residence is listed as nonhomestead, contact your county assessor immediately. Under Minnesota Statutes 275.065 subdivision 3(g), providing satisfactory documentation to the county assessor by the applicable deadline requires the assessor to reclassify qualifying property as homestead for the upcoming tax year. The statute gives no date, so ask your county assessor.

How Much Emergency Fund Do I Need? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated June 25, 2026 You need an emergency fund equal to 3 to 6 months of your essential monthly expenses, not your total income. Basing the fund on your needs alone, rather than your full paycheck, often cuts the target in half. This guide shows you how to set that number, when to hold more or less, where to keep the cash, and how to build the fund. Tools for this journey Monthly budget → 50/30/20 budget → Savings goal → Size it on essential expenses, not income Your emergency fund should cover essential monthly expenses, not your whole income. Essentials are the bills you cannot skip: rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments. Leave out the extras. Dining out, travel, subscriptions, and shopping are wants, not needs. In a real emergency, you pause those costs, so your fund does not have to replace them. This is the point most people miss. Sizing a fund on gross income can nearly double the target for no reason. Add up your true essentials first -- our budget tools make that quick -- then multiply by the number of months you want to cover. A worked example: $3,000 a month Say your essential expenses come to $3,000 a month. Three months of coverage is $9,000. Six months is $18,000. That range, $9,000 to $18,000, is your target. Pick a point in the range based on your risk. A stable two-income household might aim near $9,000. A single earner with variable pay leans toward $18,000. Use our savings goal calculator to turn that target into a monthly savings plan you can actually follow. When to hold more than the minimum Hold closer to 6 months -- or more -- when your income is less certain or harder to replace. Several situations call for a bigger cushion. **One income.** A single earner has no second paycheck as backup. **Sole earner for a family.** More people depend on that one income. **Variable or self-employed income.** Freelancers and commission earners face uneven months, so 6 to 12 months is safer. **A shaky job or industry.** If layoffs are a real risk, a longer runway buys time. **A long expected job search.** Senior or specialized roles can take many months to replace. The less predictable your income, the more months you want saved. When 3 months is enough Three months of essential expenses can be enough when your income is stable and backed up. Two steady salaries in one household are the clearest case. If one partner loses a job, the other paycheck still covers part of the bills. That shared safety net lowers how much cash you must hold. Other signs you can sit at the lower end: strong job security, an in-demand skill, and no dependents relying only on you. You can always build past 3 months later, but reaching that first milestone matters most. Where to keep your emergency fund Keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account that is FDIC-insured and easy to reach. The money must be safe and available the day you need it. The FDIC automatically insures deposits up to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank. A savings account keeps your cash protected while it earns interest. Skip investments like stocks for this money. Their value can drop right when an emergency hits. Also skip a plain checking account, where idle cash earns almost nothing and is easy to spend by accident. One caution: do not treat a credit card as your emergency fund. If you already carry a balance, see how long it takes to pay off a credit card to understand the real cost. If a bank outage causes late or overdraft fees, read what to do about bank fees after an outage for how to ask for a reversal. Build it in the right order Build your emergency fund in two stages so early progress feels reachable. First, save a small starter fund of $1,000 to $2,000. This covers most surprise bills, like a car repair or a medical copay. A starter fund also keeps a small emergency from turning into high-interest debt. Once it is in place, grow the fund toward your full 3-to-6-month target. Wondering whether to finish the fund before investing or clearing debt? See our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest to sequence the rest of your plan. Two quick self-checks beyond the dollar target A 3-to-6-month fund is the target, but two quick questions show whether you are actually secure today, not just on paper. First: could you cover a $1,000 surprise bill without touching a credit card? If the honest answer is no, you are relying on credit as a backstop, not savings. That gap matters even if your fund technically meets the 3-month minimum, since a card balance carries interest your savings never will. Second: how many weeks of essential bills could you cover the day your income stopped? Add up your checking and savings balances, then divide by your weekly essential spend from the first section above. If the number is under four weeks, treat building the starter fund as your most urgent money goal, ahead of extra debt payments or new investing. Frequently asked questions How much emergency fund do I need? You need 3 to 6 months of your essential monthly expenses, not 3 to 6 months of income. Add up rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments. Then multiply by 3 for the low end and 6 for the high end. Should an emergency fund be based on income or expenses? Expenses -- specifically your essential expenses. In an emergency you cut wants like dining out and travel, so your fund only needs to cover needs. Sizing it on your full income can nearly double the target for no reason. How much should I save before I start investing? Save a starter fund of $1,000 to $2,000 first, then build toward 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. A starter fund keeps a small emergency from becoming credit card debt before you invest or attack other debt. Where should I keep my emergency fund? In a high-yield savings account that is FDIC-insured and liquid. FDIC insurance protects deposits up to at least $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank. A savings account also lets the cash earn interest while staying easy to reach. Avoid stocks, which can fall right when you need the money. How many months should I save if I am self-employed? Aim for 6 to 12 months of essential expenses if your income is variable or self-employed. Uneven months and slow seasons make a longer cushion safer than the standard 3 to 6 months. A single earner supporting a family should also lean toward the higher end. Why do I need an emergency fund? An emergency fund keeps a surprise cost from turning into high-interest debt. The Federal Reserve found that in 2024, only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent. A dedicated fund means a car repair or medical bill does not derail your budget. How do I know if I'm secretly relying on credit instead of savings? Ask whether you could cover a $1,000 surprise bill without touching a credit card. If not, your card is functioning as your real emergency fund, and it charges interest yours never will. Building even a $1,000 starter fund removes that gap. How much emergency fund is too much? An emergency fund is too large once the balance sits well past your range, typically 6 months of essential expenses for most households or 6 to 12 for variable income. To check your numbers, add up your current monthly essential expenses, multiply by your target months, and compare that figure with your balance. Any cash above that personal target can go toward other financial goals. To sequence your next steps, see our guide on whether to pay off debt or invest . How much emergency fund should a couple or a family have? There is no separate target by household size, so couples and families still aim for 3 to 6 months of essential monthly expenses rather than income. Stable two-income households can aim near 3 months because the other paycheck still covers part of the bills, while a family's sole earner should lean toward 6 months or more. To calculate your dollar goal, add up household essentials for rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, and minimum debt payments, then multiply by your months. For example, if your household's essentials total $3,000 a month, 3 months is $9,000 and 6 months is $18,000. You can total your household essentials using our monthly budget calculator . Many buyers assume that buying a home immediately lowers their tax bill. For a married couple filing jointly in 2026, the standard deduction is $32,200, which means an average mortgage balance often generates less write-off value than taking the standard amount. Determining whether you come out ahead requires running the actual numbers on your interest, real estate taxes, and other qualified expenses before choosing Schedule A. Tools for this journey Mortgage calculator hub → Closing cost calculator → Home affordability → HELOC calculator → Do Your Deductions Beat the Standard Deduction A homeowner only benefits from deducting housing costs if their combined itemized expenses exceed the standard deduction for their tax filing status. Under the IRS inflation adjustments for tax year 2026 , the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and married individuals filing separately, $24,150 for heads of household, and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly. Unless your total itemized deductions surpass those thresholds, you claim the standard deduction instead. Consider a hypothetical worked example of a $400,000 30-year fixed mortgage at an interest rate of 6.5%. The monthly principal-and-interest payment is $2,528.27, generating roughly $25,868.36 of interest in the first full year. If that household pays $5,000 in annual property taxes, their baseline housing deductions total $30,868. For a married couple filing jointly, that $30,868 total sits below the $32,200 standard deduction, so itemizing purely on those two items yields no tax advantage. That couple would need at least $1,332 in additional itemized deductions, such as charitable gifts or state income taxes, before itemizing provides a financial gain. With smaller balances, the gap widens. A $300,000 mortgage at 6.5% has a monthly payment of $1,896.20 and generates about $19,401.27 of interest during the first year. Even with $5,000 in property taxes, the total deduction reaches $24,401.27, leaving a married couple thousands of dollars short of the $32,200 threshold. You can estimate your own amortization schedule using our mortgage calculator hub to check your specific first-year interest amount. Mortgage Interest Deductions and Debt Limits Homeowners who itemize can deduct the interest paid on debt used to acquire or substantially improve their primary or secondary residence. According to IRS Publication 936 and IRS Topic 505 , mortgage interest is deductible on acquisition debt up to $750,000 for single filers and married couples filing jointly, or $375,000 for married filers filing separately, on homes acquired after December 15, 2017. A higher grandfathered limit of $1 million, or $500,000 for married filing separately, applies to mortgages originated on or before December 15, 2017. Each January, your mortgage servicer reports the exact interest you paid during the prior calendar year on Form 1098. If your total qualifying mortgage balance across all properties exceeds the $750,000 acquisition debt limit, you cannot deduct the interest attributable to the excess balance. Review our guide on mortgage early payoff tax implications to evaluate how accelerating payments impacts your annual interest deduction. Home Equity Loan and Line of Credit Interest Interest on a home equity loan or a home equity line of credit is deductible only when the borrowed funds are spent to buy, build, or substantially improve the home that secures the loan. Per IRS Publication 936 , 'No matter when the indebtedness was incurred, you can no longer deduct the interest from a loan secured by your home to the extent the loan proceeds weren't used to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.' Any debt secured by your home also counts against the overall $750,000 acquisition indebtedness ceiling. The specific use of the loan proceeds dictates its tax deductibility. If you take out a $50,000 home equity loan to remodel your kitchen, replace a roof, or construct an addition, the interest qualifies for deduction. Conversely, if you tap home equity to consolidate personal credit card debt, finance a car purchase, or pay college tuition, none of that interest can be deducted. Explore our breakdown of HELOC vs home equity loan options and run figures through our HELOC calculator to see the monthly payment impact. Deducting Mortgage Discount Points Discount points paid upfront to lower your mortgage interest rate can be deducted on Schedule A, either immediately in the year paid or spread across the loan term. As outlined in IRS Topic 505 and IRS Publication 936 , points paid on a purchase mortgage for your primary residence can generally be deducted in full in the year you pay them if specific requirements are met. The loan must be used to purchase or build your main home, and the points must be clearly shown as points on your settlement statement. When points do not qualify for immediate full deduction, they must be deducted ratably over the life of the mortgage. Points paid by a seller cannot be deducted by the buyer as interest. To calculate upfront financing expenses on a prospective purchase, check our closing cost calculator . Property Taxes and the State and Local Tax Cap Real estate property taxes assessed by state or local governments are deductible as an itemized expense on Schedule A within statutory limits. Under IRS Topic 503 , state and local real property taxes are combined with other state and local taxes, including income or sales taxes, subject to an aggregate state and local tax deduction cap. The state and local tax deduction cap is set at $40,000 for 2025, or $20,000 for married individuals filing separately, and the cap cannot be reduced below $10,000. Under current law, this cap is scheduled to rise 1% annually, making the cap $40,400 for 2026, though filers should verify the current figure directly at IRS Topic 503 . Check the amount on your county property tax statement, because only taxes actually paid count. If you own in Minnesota, see how to read a Minnesota proposed property tax notice for what the November notice means for next year's bill. Home Office Deductions for Eligible Homeowners Homeowners who run an independent business or work as self-employed individuals may deduct qualifying home office expenses, but regular corporate employees cannot. Under rules from the IRS simplified home office option , qualified taxpayers can claim a simplified deduction of $5 per square foot for a dedicated work area, up to a maximum of 300 square feet, which produces a top deduction of $1,500. Alternatively, filers can calculate actual expenses based on the square footage percentage of housing costs, including utilities, insurance, and depreciation. To qualify under either method, the home office space must be used exclusively and on a regular basis as your principal place of business or to meet clients. Employees receiving a Form W-2 cannot claim a home office deduction under current federal rules, because miscellaneous itemized deductions for unreimbursed employee business expenses were eliminated for tax years beginning after 2017. Medically Necessary Home Improvements Capital improvements made to your home for medical care qualify as itemized medical deductions only to the extent the expense exceeds any increase in property value. According to IRS Publication 502 and IRS Topic 502 , capital expenditures made primarily for medical care, such as widening doorways, installing wheelchair ramps, lowering kitchen counters, or adding a chairlift, count toward your medical expense calculation. However, if an improvement increases the market value of your residence, the deductible amount is strictly limited to the difference between the actual construction cost and the corresponding increase in the home's appraisal value. Total qualified medical expenses are only deductible on Schedule A to the extent they exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, commonly abbreviated as AGI. For example, if your adjusted gross income is $100,000, only medical expenses exceeding $7,500 can be factored into your itemized deductions. Homeowner Expenses That Are Not Deductible Many recurring expenses associated with owning real estate do not qualify for federal tax deductions on a primary personal residence. IRS guidance specifies that regular personal housing outlays are not deductible on Schedule A: Mortgage principal payments Homeowners insurance and hazard insurance premiums Routine maintenance costs and general repairs Utilities including electricity, natural gas, trash, and water Homeowners association fees, commonly known as HOA dues Unlike capital improvements that get added to your property basis, routine repairs such as fixing a roof leak or repainting a wall do not lower your current taxable income. In addition, the itemized deduction for private mortgage insurance premiums is noted in IRS Publication 936 as expired, and tax law changes in 2025 affect this area, so consult the current version of the publication to confirm whether any recent legislation reinstates the deduction for your filing year. Filing Preparation and Recordkeeping Steps Organizing real estate documentation before tax season ensures you do not miss qualifying deductions or claim invalid write-offs. Follow these practical steps when preparing your annual filing: Gather your Form 1098 statements from all mortgage servicers that held your loan during the calendar year. Review your closing disclosure if you purchased or refinanced during the tax year to verify whether discount points were itemized. Check your county property tax statements to verify the exact tax payments disbursed within the tax year. Keep paid receipts and contractor invoices for any medical modifications or substantial improvements funded via home equity. Verify the current treatment of mortgage insurance premiums in IRS Publication 936 to check if your policy qualifies under newly enacted rules. Comparing these gathered records against the standard deduction threshold helps you decide whether filing Schedule A is worth the effort. For a broad inventory of deductions outside real estate, consult our tax deductions checklist . Who This Deductibility Math Does Not Serve The standard deduction test produces very different outcomes depending on debt balance and location. Enter your numbers above to see your target home price and monthly payment. Lenders compare your income with your debts to determine how much you can borrow. Under this rule, your monthly housing payment should stay at or below 28% of your gross monthly income, and your total debt payments should stay at or below 36%. Your gross income is what you earn before taxes. The lower of these two limits sets your real budget. The housing payment here means PITI, not just principal and interest. PITI stands for principal, interest, property taxes, and insurance. If your down payment is under 20%, lenders usually add private mortgage insurance (PMI), which raises the payment. Try our down payment calculator and closing cost calculator to plan the cash you'll need up front. One underwriting trap that stops otherwise-qualified buyers: unaddressed IRS back taxes. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac , and FHA (Handbook 4000.1) will not underwrite while there's IRS debt outstanding unless you're on a formal long-term installment agreement AND have made at least 3 monthly payments on time. A recorded Notice of Federal Tax Lien blocks approval entirely until it's released, discharged, or subordinated to the new mortgage. If back taxes are in the picture, the back taxes impact calculator shows exactly what stops the loan and how to clear each block. Once you have a price range, the home buying checklist lays out what to do and check at each stage of the purchase. A worked example Say you earn $90,000 a year, or $7,500 in gross monthly income. You pay $400 a month toward existing debt, have $40,000 for a down payment, and face a 6.5% rate on a 30-year loan. Under the 28% housing limit, your maximum monthly payment is $2,100. That is the binding limit here, so it sets your budget. With property tax near 1.1% and insurance around $1,800 a year, you can afford a home priced at about $287,000, with a loan of roughly $247,285. The $2,100 payment breaks down to about $1,563 in principal and interest, $263 in property tax, $150 in insurance, and $124 in PMI, since the down payment is under 20%. Common mistakes to avoid Budgeting for only principal and interest. Property taxes, insurance, and PMI are part of every payment and can add hundreds of dollars a month. If you are buying in Minnesota, see why a Minnesota proposed tax can change your budget . Ignoring existing debt. A car loan or student loan payment shrinks your housing budget close to dollar for dollar under the 36% limit. Treating the lender's maximum as your target. Lenders may approve a debt-to-income ratio well above 36%, but a higher ratio leaves less room for emergencies. Using take-home pay instead of gross income. The 28/36 rule is based on income before taxes, so using net pay distorts the result. Forgetting closing costs and a cash cushion.
